title: Views Created by Slicing
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of views created by slicing and name one situation where it is useful.
Apply basic indexing and views to a small NumPy example and inspect the resulting values, shape, or dtype.
Identify one important limitation, boundary case, or validation check for views created by slicing.

content.intro: This lesson develops topic 171 of the supplied curriculum: **Views Created by Slicing**. The main starting point is **Basic indexing and views**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Views and references can share memory, while copies own separate data. Awareness of this difference prevents accidental mutation and helps explain memory/performance trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Views Created by Slicing** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Basic indexing and views** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
view = a[1:4]
view[0] = 99
print(a.tolist())
content_blocks.expected_output:
Observed output in the available validation environment (Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.3.5):
[0, 99, 2, 3, 4]

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a slice owns independent memory
common_mistakes.why: Basic slicing commonly creates a view.
Short timings vary due to startup, cache, and system noise.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat measurements, use representative sizes, and compare equivalent work.
